Communion Seasons
kuh-MYOO-nyun SEE-zunz
noun phrase (Reformed pastoral practice)
Scottish-Presbyterian tradition (16th-19th centuries) of celebrating the Lord's Supper in concentrated multi-day gatherings several times per year rather than weekly or monthly. Each communion season typically included Thursday (preparation / fast day), Saturday (further preparation), Sunday (the Supper), and Monday (thanksgiving). Substantively shaped the American Presbyterian frontier-revival tradition.

📖 Biblical Definition

Scottish-Presbyterian sacramental tradition (16th-19th centuries) of celebrating the Lord's Supper in concentrated multi-day gatherings several times per year rather than weekly or monthly. The practice developed substantively in post-Reformation Scotland and substantially shaped Scottish-Presbyterian piety for three centuries. Each communion season typically included: (1) Thursday fast day (the pre-communion preparation day, with substantive sermons calling for repentance and self-examination); (2) Saturday preparation (further pre-communion sermons and self-examination); (3) Sunday Supper (the celebration of the Lord's Supper, often with multiple communion tables at large gatherings, the elders distributing communion tokens to examined-and-approved communicants in advance, the minister fencing the table with substantive exhortation, the meal celebrated with the people seated at long tables in the substantive Scottish-Presbyterian liturgical form); (4) Monday thanksgiving (the post-communion thanksgiving day with substantive sermons on the gospel benefits applied at the Table). The communion seasons drew large gatherings — sometimes thousands of people traveling substantial distances from surrounding parishes — and were substantively shaping events in Scottish-Presbyterian community life. The tradition substantially transferred to the American Presbyterian frontier; the famous Cane Ridge Revival (1801, Kentucky) was substantively a Scottish-Presbyterian communion season that overflowed its bounds and became the spark of the broader Second Great Awakening. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the communion-seasons tradition with appreciation for the substantive seriousness of the Supper it embodies and with care for the substantive theological-liturgical questions of frequency (the Calvin-Geneva tradition favored more frequent celebration; the Scottish-Presbyterian tradition favored less frequent but more substantively prepared celebration; the contemporary Reformed-confessional discussion continues).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Scottish-Presbyterian sacramental tradition (16th-19th c.) of concentrated multi-day Lord's Supper celebrations several times per year; Thursday fast / Saturday preparation / Sunday Supper / Monday thanksgiving; substantively shaped American Presbyterian frontier and Cane Ridge Revival 1801.

COMMUNION SEASONS, n. phr. (Reformed pastoral practice) Scottish-Presbyterian sacramental tradition 16th-19th c.; Lord's Supper celebrated in concentrated multi-day gatherings several times per year rather than weekly or monthly. Each communion season: (1) Thursday fast day (pre-communion preparation; sermons calling repentance and self-examination); (2) Saturday preparation; (3) Sunday Supper (often multiple communion tables, elders distributing communion tokens to examined communicants in advance, minister fencing the table); (4) Monday thanksgiving. Large gatherings — sometimes thousands — from surrounding parishes. Transferred to American Presbyterian frontier; Cane Ridge Revival 1801 substantively a Scottish-Presbyterian communion season that overflowed and sparked Second Great Awakening.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The communion-seasons tradition is largely lost in contemporary American Presbyterianism; the principal contemporary discussion involves frequency of the Lord's Supper (Geneva-Calvin frequent celebration vs. Scottish-Presbyterian less frequent but more substantively prepared celebration).

expand to see more

Communion seasons as a Scottish-Presbyterian sacramental tradition is largely lost in contemporary American Presbyterianism and broader Reformed practice. The principal contemporary discussion involves the question of frequency of the Lord's Supper: the Calvin-Geneva tradition substantively favored more frequent celebration (Calvin himself argued for weekly celebration; the Geneva pastors were limited to quarterly celebration by the City Council, against Calvin's substantive position); the Scottish-Presbyterian tradition substantively favored less frequent but more substantively prepared celebration (the multi-day communion seasons). Contemporary Reformed-confessional practice varies widely (PCA, OPC, RPCNA, Continental Reformed denominations have varying frequencies). The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the question with care: the substantive seriousness of the Supper that the communion-seasons tradition embodied is a substantive theological-pastoral substance to be recovered, regardless of which frequency-arrangement a particular Reformed-confessional church adopts.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Scottish-Presbyterian tradition 16th-19th c.; concentrated multi-day Lord's Supper celebrations; transferred to American Presbyterian frontier; Cane Ridge Revival 1801.
